title: Federal Judge Clears Trump to End Deportation Protections for Somali Nationals
excerpt: A Boston judge lifted a stay blocking the termination of Temporary Protected Status for Somalia, citing the Supreme Court's June ruling that sharply limited judicial review of such decisions.
body:
• U.S. District Judge Allison Burroughs lifted a stay preventing DHS from ending TPS for Somalia, affecting up to 2,471 current holders and 1,383 with pending applications
  • The ruling follows the Supreme Court's June decision in Mullin v. Doe, which curtailed lower courts' ability to block TPS terminations on non-constitutional grounds
  • TPS for South Sudan and Myanmar was similarly ended last week; only Ethiopia's designation remains blocked by a judge
  • The Trump administration has moved to terminate TPS for nationals of 13 countries that provided humanitarian immigration protections

A federal judge on Friday cleared the way for the Trump administration to strip Somali nationals of legal protections against deportation, removing one of the last judicial barriers to the administration's systematic dismantling of the Temporary Protected Status program.

U.S. District Judge Allison Burroughs in Boston lifted a stay that had prevented the Department of Homeland Security from terminating Somalia's TPS designation, according to Reuters. The decision affects up to 2,471 Somali nationals currently holding TPS and another 1,383 with pending applications, according to U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services data cited by Fox News.

The Legal Path

Burroughs, an appointee of former President Barack Obama, had initially blocked the termination in March after a lawsuit by four Somali nationals and two advocacy groups, including African Communities Together. The plaintiffs argued the administration sought to end TPS for Somalia due to bias against non-white immigrants, pointing to Trump's past descriptions of Somalis as "garbage" and "low IQ people."

https://x.com/ResisttheMS/status/2088669854228516959

The case turned on the U.S. Supreme Court's June ruling in Mullin v. Doe, which held that the TPS statute bars judicial review of certain non-constitutional decisions to terminate designations. The 6-3 ruling, powered by the court's conservative majority, curtailed the ability of lower courts to block DHS actions across the program.

"Plaintiffs have made a convincing showing that they will suffer irreparable harm if the injunction is withheld … and the balance of hardships and the public interest also favor Plaintiffs."

— Judge Allison Burroughs, in her ruling lifting the stay

Despite those findings, Burroughs wrote she was "bound … to view things through the Mullin prism" and lifted the stay, allowing the termination to proceed.

A Broader Campaign

Somalia's TPS termination is part of a wider pattern. Former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem announced plans to end the designation in January, arguing Somalia's conditions had improved — despite ongoing fighting between Somali forces and al-Shabaab militants.

Two other judges last week allowed the administration to end TPS for South Sudan and Myanmar. Only Ethiopia's designation remains blocked. The administration has moved to terminate TPS for nationals of 13 countries that had provided humanitarian immigration protections, according to Reuters.

The plaintiffs filed an amended complaint after the Supreme Court ruling, raising Fifth Amendment equal protection claims alleging racial and national-origin discrimination. Burroughs issued a brief administrative stay earlier this month while considering those claims, but ultimately concluded the Supreme Court's decision constrained her ability to continue blocking the action.

Impact on Immigrant Communities

TPS has allowed Somali nationals to live and work legally in the United States since the program was first extended to Somalia in 1991, during the country's civil war. The termination could expose those without another lawful immigration status to deportation.

For South Asian and other immigrant communities watching closely, the case reinforces how the Supreme Court's Mullin ruling has reshaped the legal landscape for TPS challenges nationwide. The decision effectively closes the door on most judicial challenges to TPS terminations, leaving Congressional action as the primary remaining avenue for protection.

What's Next

The plaintiffs' constitutional claims remain technically alive, but the practical impact is immediate: DHS can now move to end TPS for Somali nationals. The broader question is whether Congress will act to provide a pathway for long-term TPS holders who have built lives in the U.S. over decades — or whether the program's beneficiaries across all 13 targeted countries will face the same outcome.
nri_angle: The Supreme Court's Mullin ruling reshapes the legal landscape for TPS challenges, with implications for South Asian and other immigrant communities.
